questions.question: What is an interface in C#?
options: A contract defining members a type must implement, with no implementation
A class that can't be instantiated
A type of struct
A base class with optional methods
questions.explanation: An interface defines a contract — method and property signatures with no implementation (prior to C# 8 default interface methods). Any type that implements the interface must provide the implementation.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about interfaces in C#?
options: They can have method signatures
They can have instance fields
A class can implement multiple interfaces
They can be instantiated directly
questions.explanation: Interfaces support multiple implementation but cannot have instance fields and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions.question: What does polymorphism allow you to do?
options: Hide class fields from subclasses
Treat different types through a shared base type or interface
Prevent a class from being inherited
Define multiple constructors on a class
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets you write code against a base type or interface and have different behaviour at runtime depending on the actual type.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `abstract` keyword on a class?
options: It makes all methods private
It prevents the class from being inherited
It prevents the class from being instantiated directly
It makes the class static
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly — they are meant to be inherited and their abstract members overridden.

questions.question: What are the differences between an abstract class and an interface?
options: Abstract classes can have constructors
Interfaces can have instance fields
A class can inherit multiple abstract classes
Abstract classes can have implemented methods
questions.explanation: Abstract classes can have constructors and fully implemented methods. Interfaces cannot have instance fields, and C# does not support multiple class inheritance.

questions.question: What does the `sealed` keyword do to a class?
options: Prevents it from being instantiated
Prevents it from being inherited
Makes all its members private
Makes it a singleton
questions.explanation: A sealed class cannot be used as a base class — no other class can inherit from it. This also allows the JIT to make certain optimisations.

questions.question: What is required for a subclass to override a method from its base class?
options: The method must be public
The base method must be marked virtual or abstract, and the subclass uses override
The subclass must be sealed
The base class must be abstract
questions.explanation: The base class method must be marked virtual (or abstract). The subclass then uses the override keyword. Without virtual, the base method cannot be properly overridden.

questions.question: What does the `new` keyword do when used on a method in a subclass?
options: Forces the override of a virtual method
Hides the base class method without polymorphic dispatch
Creates a new instance of the class
Prevents the method from being inherited further
questions.explanation: The new keyword hides the base class method. Unlike override, polymorphism does not apply — calling through a base type reference will call the base method, not the hidden one.

questions.question: What does the `base` keyword allow you to do?
options: Access the base class constructor or overridden member from within a subclass
Make a method call as fast as a direct call
Access private fields of the base class
Prevent further inheritance
questions.explanation: base lets you call a base class constructor (base(...)) or access an overridden member (base.Method()) from within a derived class.

questions.question: What is the core difference between a struct and a class in C#?
options: Structs support inheritance
Structs are value types, classes are reference types
Classes are stored on the stack
There is no meaningful difference
questions.explanation: Structs are value types — they are copied on assignment and typically stack-allocated. Classes are reference types — variables hold a reference to a heap allocation.

questions.question: What does the `static` keyword mean on a method?
options: The method can only be called once
The method belongs to the type, not an instance
The method cannot return a value
The method is thread-safe
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the type itself and are called without creating an instance. They cannot access instance (non-static) members.

questions.question:
What is the output of this code?
`int x = 5; Console.WriteLine(x++);`
options: Compile error
questions.explanation: The post-increment operator (x++) returns the current value first, then increments. So 5 is printed, then x becomes 6.

questions.question: What does `int?` mean in C#?
options: An int that defaults to zero
A nullable int that can hold an int value or null
An optional parameter
An int that throws if accessed when unset
questions.explanation: int? is shorthand for Nullable<int>. It can hold any int value or null, and exposes .HasValue and .Value properties.

questions.question: What are the differences between `ref` and `out` parameters?
options: ref requires the variable to be initialised before passing
out requires the variable to be assigned inside the method
ref and out are identical
out variables do not need to be initialised before passing
questions.explanation: ref requires the caller to initialise the variable first. out does not require prior initialisation but the method must assign it before returning. Both pass by reference.

questions.question: Why is string concatenation with `+` in a tight loop a performance concern?
options: Strings use a fixed-size buffer that overflows
Each concatenation creates a new string allocation on the heap
The + operator is not overloaded for strings
String comparison is O(n) which slows the loop
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable in C#. Every + creates a new string object. In a loop this generates significant garbage. Use StringBuilder or string.Join for repeated concatenation.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about `List<T>` in C#?
options: It has a fixed size
It is generic
Elements can be accessed by index
It only stores reference types
questions.explanation: List<T> is generic and supports index access. It is dynamic in size and can store both value and reference types.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of a key lookup in a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`?
options: O(n) — it scans all entries
O(log n) — it uses a binary search
O(1) — amortized constant time via hashing
O(n log n) — it sorts keys first
questions.explanation: Dictionary uses a hash table. Key lookup is O(1) amortised — it hashes the key and goes directly to the bucket, without scanning other entries.

questions.question: When should you prefer `HashSet<T>` over `List<T>`?
options: When order of elements matters
When you need fast Contains checks and don't need duplicates or index access
When storing value types only
When the collection is small
questions.explanation: HashSet provides O(1) Contains. List.Contains is O(n). Use HashSet when you frequently check membership and don't need ordering or duplicates.

questions.question: What is the advantage of `Dictionary.TryGetValue` over checking `ContainsKey` then accessing by key?
options: TryGetValue is more readable
TryGetValue avoids a double lookup by combining the check and retrieval in one operation
ContainsKey throws if the key is missing
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Calling ContainsKey then indexing performs two hash lookups. TryGetValue does it in one, returning the value directly in an out parameter.

questions.question: When is a LINQ query with `Where` actually executed?
options: When the query is written
When it is assigned to a variable
When the result is enumerated (e.g. in a foreach or .ToList())
When the source collection changes
questions.explanation: LINQ uses deferred execution. The query is a description of what to do, not the result. Execution happens when you iterate — e.g. foreach, ToList(), Count().

questions.question: Why should you avoid LINQ in performance-critical code like Update loops?
options: LINQ queries execute on a background thread
LINQ methods allocate iterators and closures on the heap, creating garbage
LINQ does not support generic types
LINQ throws in IL2CPP builds
questions.explanation: Each LINQ method allocates enumerator objects. Closures in lambdas may also allocate. In a tight loop this creates GC pressure. For hot paths, use manual loops.

questions.question: What does `FirstOrDefault` return if no element matches the predicate?
options: It throws an InvalidOperationException
null for reference types, default value for value types
An empty collection
The last element
questions.explanation: FirstOrDefault returns the default value of the type if nothing matches — null for reference types, 0 for int, etc. First() would throw instead.

questions.question: What is `Action` in C#?
options: A built-in coroutine type
A generic delegate type that takes no return value
A Unity lifecycle method
An async task wrapper
questions.explanation: Action is a built-in generic delegate for methods that return void. Action<T> takes one parameter, Action<T1,T2> takes two, and so on.

questions.question: How does `Func<int, bool>` differ from `Action<int>`?
options: Func takes no parameters
Func has a return type — the last type parameter is the return type
Action can return values, Func cannot
They are identical
questions.explanation: Func always has a return type as its last type parameter. Func<int, bool> takes an int and returns a bool. Action always returns void.

questions.question: Why is it important to unsubscribe from events when an object is destroyed?
options: Events hold strong references to subscribers, preventing garbage collection and causing null reference calls
Events become invalid after the first call
The event system will throw if a subscriber is destroyed
Unity automatically unsubscribes all events
questions.explanation: An event holds a reference to the delegate, which holds a reference to the subscriber. If the subscriber is destroyed but not unsubscribed, it cannot be GC'd and the event will attempt to call a dead object.

questions.question: You subscribe to an event twice with the same method. How many times will that method be called when the event fires?
options: Once — duplicates are ignored
Twice — delegates are multicast and maintain all subscriptions
It throws an exception
It depends on the event keyword
questions.explanation: Delegates are multicast — adding the same method twice creates two invocations. Always guard subscribe calls or use -= before += to avoid accidental double-subscription.

questions.question: What does the `async` keyword do to a method?
options: Makes it run on a background thread immediately
Allows the method to use await and returns a Task
Makes it run faster
Converts it to a coroutine
questions.explanation: async enables the use of await inside the method and wraps the return value in a Task (or Task<T>). It does not by itself put anything on a background thread.

questions.question: What does `await` do when applied to a Task?
options: Blocks the current thread until the Task completes
Suspends the current method and returns control to the caller until the Task completes
Runs the Task on a new thread
Cancels the Task if it takes too long
questions.explanation: await suspends the async method at that point, returning control to the caller without blocking the thread. Execution resumes after the Task completes.

questions.question: What does `ConfigureAwait(false)` do?
options: Disables exception handling on the Task
Tells the awaiter not to capture the current synchronisation context, allowing continuation on any thread
Makes the Task fire-and-forget
Forces the continuation onto the main thread
questions.explanation: By default await captures the synchronisation context (e.g. Unity main thread) and resumes there. ConfigureAwait(false) skips this, allowing the continuation to run on any available thread. Use it in library code, but be careful in Unity — most Unity API calls must be on the main thread.

questions.question: Which of the following are advantages of async/await over Unity coroutines?
options: Async methods can return values directly
Async supports proper exception propagation with try/catch
Async runs off the main thread by default
Async works outside of MonoBehaviour
questions.explanation: Async/await can return values (Task<T>), properly propagate exceptions, and work in non-MonoBehaviour classes. Coroutines can only signal completion via callbacks. Async does not run off the main thread by default — that requires Task.Run or a thread pool.

questions.question: What is a `CancellationToken` used for in async code?
options: To set a timeout duration on a Task
To signal to an async operation that it should stop early
To catch exceptions from cancelled Tasks
To run a Task on a specific thread
questions.explanation: A CancellationToken is passed into async methods so the caller can signal cancellation. The method checks IsCancellationRequested or calls ThrowIfCancellationRequested to abort cleanly.

questions.question: What is the risk of calling an async method without awaiting it (fire-and-forget)?
options: The method runs synchronously instead
Exceptions thrown inside the method are silently swallowed
The method runs twice
The Task is immediately cancelled
questions.explanation: If you don't await a Task, exceptions thrown inside it are not observed and will be silently lost (or in some runtimes, rethrown on a finalizer thread). Always handle exceptions in fire-and-forget patterns.

questions.question: What triggers the garbage collector in C#?
options: Calling GC.Collect() manually only
Allocating enough objects to fill a generation heap threshold
Every frame in Unity
Reference types going out of scope
questions.explanation: The GC runs when a generation's allocation budget is exhausted. In Unity this can cause frame spikes. Reducing heap allocations (new, boxing, closures, LINQ) keeps GC pressure low.

questions.question: What is boxing in C#?
options: Wrapping a method in a delegate
Copying a value type into a heap-allocated object wrapper
Casting between reference types
Allocating an array of value types
questions.explanation: Boxing wraps a value type (like int, bool, struct) in an object on the heap. It happens implicitly when passing value types to object parameters or non-generic collections. It causes heap allocation and should be avoided in hot paths.

questions.question: What problem does an object pool solve?
options: Thread synchronisation between objects
Frequent allocation and deallocation causing GC pressure
Preventing objects from being accidentally destroyed
Managing scene loading order
questions.explanation: An object pool pre-allocates objects and recycles them instead of creating and destroying. This avoids repeated heap allocations and GC collection spikes — critical for frequently spawned objects like bullets or particles.

questions.question: What does the Singleton pattern guarantee?
options: That a class cannot be subclassed
That only one instance of a class exists and provides a global access point
That all methods are thread-safe
That the class is always initialised before other classes
questions.explanation: Singleton ensures a single instance of a class and provides a static access point to it. In Unity it's commonly implemented in Awake with a static Instance property.

questions.question: What problem does the Observer pattern solve?
options: Managing object lifecycle
Decoupling a publisher from its subscribers so the publisher doesn't need to know who is listening
Ensuring only one object handles an event
Caching expensive computations
questions.explanation: Observer lets objects subscribe to events without the publisher having direct references to them. C# events and UnityEvents are built-in implementations of this pattern.
